passage: At 3 a.m. in her Pune flat, Chandrika walked the hallway with her crying baby and thought of her own father, Amandeep, who had done this with three children and a long bus commute. She remembered him falling asleep over his tea, and her fury when he missed her school recital. Now the fury had a crack in it. In the morning Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha. "You look tired, beta," he said. She nearly cried. "Papa, how did you manage us?" He laughed. "Badly, some days." She said quietly, "I'm going to be home for my child's recitals, Papa, even if I have to move a meeting." He nodded, said nothing, and pressed the tiffin into her hands. Her respect for him had grown. So had the ache.

qa.q: What did Amandeep bring in the morning?
qa.a: Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha.

qa.q: What is Chandrika feeling toward her father as she walks the hallway at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: New tenderness mixed with old hurt: the fury 'had a crack in it', and she nearly cried when he called her tired.

qa.q: What does Chandrika decide to do differently from her father?
qa.a: She resolves to be home for her child's recitals, even if she has to move a meeting.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt hearing Chandrika ask how he managed?
qa.a: Amandeep may have felt seen but a little exposed; he laughed and admitted 'Badly, some days,' then pressed the tiffin into her hands without a word.

grounding: A new parent starts to see how hard her own parents had it, feels tenderness and leftover anger, and still names what she will do differently.

passage: Miss it? Of course I miss it, Anand. I'm Tarun, and eleven-hour days, client dinners, the feeling that I was going somewhere fast, all of that was mine. My daughter is eight months old, and some evenings I sit in the nursery and grieve a life that no longer fits, then feel guilty for grieving. That guilt is the worst part. Both things are true: I love her more than I knew a person could, and I miss my old pace. For a while I pretended to feel only joy. Then I started blocking out Saturday mornings for the cycling club, no apology. I came back lighter. I still lead the design team, just differently. The old me isn't gone. It has a smaller room now, in a bigger house.

qa.q: How old is Tarun's daughter?
qa.a: Tarun's daughter is eight months old.

qa.q: Why does Tarun feel guilty when grieving the old life?
qa.a: Tarun loves the baby deeply, so missing the old pace feels like a betrayal of that love, though Tarun says both feelings are true.

qa.q: What did Tarun do to make time for himself?
qa.a: Tarun blocked out Saturday mornings for the cycling club, with no apology.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun had kept pretending to feel only joy?
qa.a: The grief would probably stay hidden and grow beside the guilt; Tarun says the cycling club made Tarun lighter.

grounding: A new parent misses old freedom and career pace, feels guilty about it, and finds time for personal interests so that a new identity includes the old one.

passage:
The facilitator at the community-centre parents' group handed out a blank sheet: "Write down everything that keeps the baby's day running." Uday, a new father, started writing and didn't stop: feed times, nappy stock, the vaccination card, calling the paediatrician, washing bottles at midnight, remembering the cotton wool. Harsha, sitting beside Uday, glanced across. "I didn't know there was that much."

Uday felt anger rise, and the old invisible feeling, but kept a level voice. "I didn't either, until I wrote it. Can we split this list, not just have you help me? I'd like you to own the vaccination card and the bottle washing, start to finish."

Harsha read the list again and nodded slowly. "Give me those two. And tell me when I've missed something, without keeping score." On the walk home Uday said, "Thank you for reading it properly."

qa.q: What did the facilitator ask the parents to write?
qa.a: The facilitator asked them to write down everything that keeps the baby's day running.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling as the list grew?
qa.a: Uday felt anger and the old invisible feeling, yet kept a level voice.

qa.q: What did Uday ask Harsha to do, and how is that different from asking for help?
qa.a: Uday asked Harsha to own the vaccination card and the bottle washing, start to finish, which makes it Harsha's responsibility rather than a favour.

qa.q: How might Harsha have seen the load before reading the list?
qa.a: Harsha seemed surprised ('I didn't know there was that much'), suggesting the work was unseen rather than ignored on purpose.

grounding: A parent whose partner does not see the unseen baby work names the tasks on a list and asks for shared ownership without martyrdom.

passage:
Dear Yamini,

I'm writing because I couldn't say it on the phone. Every time Mausi's family visits, I count what they do that I don't: homemade purée, picture books, a baby who sleeps through the night. Then I scroll through other people's posts and find more, and I close the screen feeling like never enough. Last night I sat in the dark thinking about it until it hurt.

This morning the paediatrician said the baby is growing well and asked about our routine. Bath, a story, sleep, same order every night. The paediatrician said steady is what children need. I'd forgotten that steady, loving and imperfect is a whole plan. So I'm keeping our small routines and I'll stop comparing them with other people's photos.

Thank you for always answering my late messages.

Ramesh

qa.q: What is the order of the baby's routine every night?
qa.a: Bath, a story, sleep, same order every night.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel after scrolling through other people's posts?
qa.a: Ramesh closes the screen feeling like never enough, anxious about measuring up.

qa.q: What does Ramesh decide to do about the comparisons?
qa.a: Ramesh will keep the small routines and stop comparing them with other people's photos, trusting the paediatrician's reassurance.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Yamini may feel trusted, since Ramesh could not say it on the phone, and may see that a perfect-looking life online can hide doubts.

grounding: A parent compares with relatives and social media, feels never enough, then remembers children need steady, loving, imperfect parents and trusts routines and the paediatrician.

passage:
For the fourth time that morning, the toddler tipped the steel tumbler and watched the water run across the veranda floor. Shalini felt her patience thin like old cloth. "Again?" she said, louder than she meant. The toddler looked up, startled, lip trembling. Shalini's hand was tight on the mop. She set the mop down, walked to the store-room doorway, and breathed slowly, counting to ten with her eyes on the mango tree.

From the fence, Kavitha, the neighbour, called, "They aren't plotting against you, you know. They're testing what water does." Shalini laughed despite herself. She came back and crouched, voice low. "Water stays in the tumbler. On the floor, we use the cloth together." The toddler grabbed the cloth and wiped, splashing happily. The floor stayed wet, but the morning softened.

qa.q: How many times had the toddler tipped the tumbler that morning?
qa.a: It was the fourth time that morning.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she said 'Again?' louder than she meant?
qa.a: Her patience was thinning and she was tense and frustrated, shown by her tight grip on the mop.

qa.q: What did Shalini do to avoid shouting?
qa.a: She set down the mop, stepped to the store-room doorway, breathed slowly and counted to ten, then came back and spoke in a low voice.

qa.q: How might the toddler have experienced Shalini's louder voice?
qa.a: The toddler was startled and the lip trembled, since the toddler was exploring what water does, not trying to upset anyone. 🙂

grounding: A parent whose toddler keeps testing her patience breathes, steps away for a minute, lowers her voice and treats the child as learning, not plotting.

passage:
In the checkout queue of a Bengaluru supermarket, Leela's four-year-old dropped to the floor and screamed for a plastic dinosaur. Heads turned. Seema, two places behind with a basket, raised her eyebrows. Leela's cheeks burned, and for a second she wanted to hiss. "Enough!" slipped out sharp before she crouched, moved the trolley wheel away from the child's kicking foot, and said quietly, "I'm here. We're not buying it today."

She waited, hand steady, while the screaming ran itself out. Seema muttered, "Some days are like that," and looked away kindly.

At home, Leela sat beside the child. "I was embarrassed in the shop, and my voice got sharp. I'm sorry about that." The child leaned against her and asked for the dinosaur once more, then for a story.

qa.q: What did the child scream for in the checkout queue?
qa.a: The child screamed for a plastic dinosaur.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling in the queue?
qa.a: Embarrassed and furious; her cheeks burned and for a second she wanted to hiss at the child.

qa.q: What did Leela do to repair things at home?
qa.a: She sat beside the child and apologised for the sharp 'Enough!', explaining that she had been embarrassed.

qa.q: How might Seema have seen the scene?
qa.a: Seema seems sympathetic: after raising eyebrows, Seema says 'Some days are like that' and looks away kindly.

grounding: A parent embarrassed and furious by a public tantrum stays calm, keeps the child safe, waits, and repairs later after one sharp word.

passage:
Tuesday night. I snapped at my son Sachin today. The juice went over my laptop and I said, "Can't you ever be careful?" in a voice I hate. His face closed like a shut door. He is five.

I wiped the laptop with shaking hands and felt sick. At bedtime I sat on his bed. "I shouted about the juice. That wasn't fair. Spills happen. I was worried about my work and it came out at you." He whispered, "Are you still cross?" I said no and hugged him.

Then on the way home I nearly bought him the big set of blocks to make up for it. I put it back. The hug was the repair, not a toy.

Tomorrow: breakfast together, no rush.

Kashish

qa.q: What did Kashish say when the juice went over the laptop?
qa.a: Kashish said, 'Can't you ever be careful?'

qa.q: How did Kashish feel after snapping?
qa.a: Sick and awful; Kashish's hands were shaking while wiping the laptop.

qa.q: What did Kashish do to repair, and what did Kashish choose not to do?
qa.a: Kashish apologised plainly at bedtime, naming the shouting and the worry about work, and put back the big set of blocks instead of buying forgiveness.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Kashish shouted?
qa.a: Sachin's face closed like a shut door, suggesting hurt and fear, and Sachin later whispered to ask whether Kashish was still cross.

grounding: A parent who snapped at a child feels awful, apologises simply, names what happened and reconnects without overindulging.

passage:
Note to file, community pool, Saturday junior class. Rashmi, age six, stood on the shallow-end steps for most of the session, glancing at the bench where Jeevan sat with a towel folded on one knee. Whenever Rashmi moved toward the ropes, Jeevan stood halfway up.

After class I chatted with Jeevan, who said, "I know I hover. I keep picturing the worst." I suggested one small experiment: sit on the far bench next week.

The next Saturday Jeevan sat there, hands clenched. Rashmi took two steps into the water, then a third, and looked back. Jeevan lifted a thumb but stayed seated. Rashmi's grin was wide.

Farida, swim coach

qa.q: Where did Jeevan sit the following Saturday?
qa.a: Jeevan sat on the far bench.

qa.q: What is Jeevan worried about?
qa.a: Jeevan keeps picturing the worst, which is why Jeevan stood halfway up whenever Rashmi moved toward the ropes.

qa.q: What small step helped Jeevan let Rashmi try?
qa.a: Farida suggested sitting on the far bench, and Jeevan tried it and stayed seated even with hands clenched.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rashmi to be watched so closely?
qa.a: Rashmi stayed on the steps glancing at the bench, as if waiting for permission; with room to move, Rashmi took steps into the water and grinned.

grounding: A parent's anxious hovering holds a child back at the pool; the parent recognises the worry and allows a small risk so the child can build courage.

passage:
In the paediatric clinic waiting room, Asif's phone showed a cousin's video: a toddler the same age, counting to twenty. Asif looked at their own child, who was stacking two blocks and babbling, and felt a tight worry. In the consulting room Asif said, "My cousin's baby already counts. Ours barely says five words. Should I be worried?"

Dr Karthik smiled and asked what the child did at home. Pointed at things, waved, laughed when hidden behind a cloth. "Every child finds their own speed," Dr Karthik said. "If it keeps worrying you, we can arrange a proper check."

Asif nodded, relieved and a bit embarrassed. That evening Asif clapped for the two-block tower and didn't mention the cousin once.

qa.q: What did the cousin's toddler do in the video?
qa.a: The toddler counted to twenty.

qa.q: What worries Asif when comparing the two children?
qa.a: Asif worries that their own child, who barely says five words, is behind the cousin's child.

qa.q: What did Asif do that worked better than comparing aloud?
qa.a: Asif took the worry to Dr Karthik, listened, and at home clapped for the two-block tower without mentioning the cousin.

qa.q: How might the child feel if Asif kept comparing them with cousins?
qa.a: The child could come to feel measured and not good enough, whereas the clap for the tower shows delight in the child's own pace.

grounding: A parent compares a child with a cousin and feels anxious, asks a professional, hears that every child finds their own speed, and avoids shaming comparison.

passage:
Saturday. At the school fair, Pranav held up a phone to show everyone the painting and first-prize certificate of Pranav's daughter Vidya. "Did you see her maths marks too?" Pranav asked a neighbour. Vidya tugged Pranav's sleeve, cheeks red.

Tuesday. At dinner Vidya said, "You only clap when I win." Pranav paused, fork in the air. "That's not true." Then the fair came back to mind. "Tell me one thing you did this week that you're proud of." Vidya said, "I helped Meera when she fell, and I kept trying the hard puzzle even when it was annoying."

Sunday. Pranav asked to see the unfinished puzzle. "You kept at it. I love watching you try." Vidya beamed. Pranav had once dreamed of being a painter and, this time, didn't say a word about brushes.

qa.q: What did Pranav show everyone at the school fair?
qa.a: Pranav showed everyone Vidya's painting and first-prize certificate.

qa.q: Why did Vidya tug Pranav's sleeve with red cheeks?
qa.a: Vidya seems embarrassed by the showing off, and later says 'You only clap when I win,' suggesting feeling valued for results.

qa.q: What did Pranav change after Tuesday's dinner?
qa.a: Pranav asked what Vidya was proud of and began praising effort, like keeping at the puzzle and helping Meera, rather than prizes.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Vidya said, "You only clap when I win"?
qa.a: Pranav seemed caught off guard, pausing with the fork in the air and denying it, before remembering the fair and changing how Pranav praised Vidya.

grounding: A parent proud of their child shifts praise from marks and prizes to effort and character and keeps their own unfulfilled dreams out of it.
